config.title: Number of Islands

intro.title: Number of Islands
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that counts the number of islands in a 2D grid map, where '1' represents land and '0' represents water. The core programming concept is depth-first search (DFS), a fundamental graph traversal algorithm used to explore connected land cells. You will use JavaScript arrays to represent the grid and implement recursion or a stack for the DFS traversal. This exercise will help you understand how to solve lessons involving connected components in a grid, a common pattern in algorithmic challenges.
intro.usecase: The 'Number of Islands' algorithm is a foundational pattern for analyzing connected regions in grid-based data, directly applicable to real-world mapping and image processing software. For example, in a geographic information system (GIS) dashboard, it can count distinct landmasses from satellite imagery data displayed on an interactive map panel. Developers use this to build features like terrain analysis tools or to segment medical images in diagnostic UIs, where identifying separate regions is critical for accurate processing and visualization.

objectives: Implement a depth-first search (DFS) function to traverse a grid representation of islands and water
Initialize and manipulate a 2D grid data structure to represent the map of islands
Apply boundary checking logic to prevent traversal beyond grid edges
Construct a main algorithm that iterates through all grid cells to count islands
Configure visited tracking to mark cells that have been explored during traversal
Update the grid state by marking visited land cells to avoid redundant counting
Integrate the DFS traversal with the main counting loop to produce the final island count

content.body: Imagine you're exploring a map of islands and ocean. Your task is to count how many separate islands exist. We'll learn how to systematically explore a grid while avoiding going in circles—a fundamental graph algorithm skill.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply depth-first search (DFS) to traverse connected land cells
• Implement visited tracking to prevent infinite loops
• Explain why marking visited cells immediately prevents cycles
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body:
Look at this 3×3 grid where '1' is land and '0' is water. How many separate islands do you see? (An island is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.)

1 1 0
0 1 0
0 0 1

Take a moment to trace the connections. When you're ready, continue to see if we agree.
content.title: Explore the grid

content.body: You likely found 2 islands: one in the top-left area (three connected '1's) and one isolated '1' at bottom-right. Notice how you mentally marked cells as 'already counted' while exploring. That's exactly what we need to automate!
content.title: Check your count

content.body: You visually scanned the grid, identified land cells, and explored their neighbors without revisiting cells you'd already seen. This manual process works for small grids but becomes impossible for large ones.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With a 100×100 grid, you can't keep track mentally. Worse, if you explore without marking visited cells, you might go in circles forever when land forms loops. We need a systematic method that remembers where we've been.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Graph algorithms explore networks by visiting connected nodes. The critical rule: mark a node as 'visited' the moment you first encounter it. This prevents infinite loops in cycles and ensures each island is counted exactly once.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of leaving breadcrumbs on paths you've walked. If you see your own breadcrumb, you know you've been here before and shouldn't walk that path again.

content.body: We'll scan the grid cell by cell. When we find unvisited land, we increment our island count and use Depth-First Search (DFS) to explore all connected land cells, marking each as visited during exploration. This ensures we fully map each island before moving on.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize island count = 0 and a visited tracking structure
2. Loop through every cell in the grid
3. If cell is land AND not visited:
   • Increment island count
   • Start DFS from that cell to visit all connected land cells
   • Mark each visited cell immediately during DFS
4. Return island count
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up grid traversal
steps.instruction: Create the main function skeleton that will accept a grid and return the island count. Initialize the count variable.
steps.hint: Remember the grid is a 2D array where grid[row][col] is either '1' or '0'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you declare the function with the correct name and parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's begin with the basic function structure: 'function numIslands(grid) { ... }'

steps.title: Add dimensions check
steps.instruction: Add a guard clause at the beginning: if the grid is empty or has no rows, return 0 immediately.
steps.hint: Check if grid is falsy or if grid.length === 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Check both if grid doesn't exist and if it has zero rows.

steps.title: Get grid dimensions
steps.instruction: Store the number of rows and columns in variables after the guard clause.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Remember to get both row count and column count from the grid.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: const rows = grid.length; const cols = grid[0].length;

steps.title: Create visited tracking
steps.instruction: Initialize a 2D boolean array with the same dimensions as grid to track visited cells. All values should start as false.
steps.hint: Use nested loops or Array.from() to create rows × cols matrix of false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure you create a proper 2D array with all values set to false.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: const visited = Array.from({length: rows}, () => Array(cols).fill(false));

steps.title: Add main traversal loop
steps.instruction: Add nested loops to iterate through every cell (row from 0 to rows-1, col from 0 to cols-1).
steps.hint: Use for loops: for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) and inside for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++).
steps.expectedOutcome: Nested loops iterating through all cells
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we can examine each cell in the grid.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure both loops go from 0 to rows-1 and 0 to cols-1 respectively.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: for (let r = 0; r < rows; r++) { for (let c = 0; c < cols; c++) { } }

steps.title: Implement DFS helper function
steps.instruction: Before the main loops, add a DFS function that takes (r, c) and explores connected land cells. It should mark the current cell as visited and recursively call itself for valid unvisited land neighbors.
steps.hint: DFS should: 1) Mark visited[r][c] = true, 2) Check four directions (up, down, left, right) if they're within bounds, are land, and not visited.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Remember to check boundaries and mark visited before recursing.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: function dfs(r, c) { visited[r][c] = true; const directions = [[-1,0],[1,0],[0,-1],[0,1]]; for (let [dr, dc] of directions) { const nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc; if (nr >= 0 && nr < rows && nc >= 0 && nc < cols && grid[nr][nc] === '1' && !visited[nr][nc]) dfs(nr, nc); } }

steps.title: Complete the algorithm
steps.instruction: Inside the nested loops, add the logic: if current cell is land ('1') and not visited, increment count and call dfs(r, c).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you check for land and unvisited before incrementing count.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented the Number of Islands algorithm using DFS with visited tracking. Remember: always mark cells as visited when you first encounter them to prevent infinite loops in cyclic graphs. This pattern applies to many graph lessons—explore connected components while avoiding revisits.
content.title: Done
